reading.title: Original Reading Studio · Day 80: Business And Sustainability
reading.passage:
A discussion of business and sustainability can become confusing when the terms of the debate are left undefined. Researchers need to separate the question they can investigate from the wider questions that remain open. The team therefore returned to the original question and checked whether its measures still represented the issue it intended to examine.

The evidence came from a defined exercise at a university study group. The report records the scale of the work and the procedure used: In a scenario linked to “ESG should be boiled down to one simple measure: emissions”, observers at a university study group followed 33 participants for 3 weeks. The initial investigation used short structured interviews as its primary research method. It tracked accuracy and confidence, not a vague impression of success. That distinction matters because an investigation is only as useful as the relationship between its question, its measure and the data actually collected.

The observations were not entirely uniform. Initially, the approach showed a modest improvement, whereas the later stage the second approach was more consistent. Some participants adapted quickly and others did not. This uneven pattern encouraged the team to examine the conditions around the task instead of presenting the average result as if it described every individual.

The authors also identify a weakness in the evidence base. The field record notes that the sample was self-selected. Such a limitation matters when a result is used to justify a wider policy. The same procedure might produce a different outcome in a setting with different resources, participants or institutional expectations. The relevant factual statement is also clear: They used short structured interviews and recorded accuracy and confidence.

A later exercise broadened the discussion. The fictional programme at a local research partnership followed 31 participants across 7 review points. Because this was a separate phase, its sample and review points must be read independently. The purpose is to practise comparing evidence carefully: identify the group, the duration and the measure before deciding whether two results are genuinely comparable.

The paragraph on interpretation makes a distinction that is often lost in public debate. Although the results for business and sustainability changed, the comparison does not demonstrate that the intervention alone produced that change. The result may be important, but the cause remains uncertain. A fair analysis considers competing explanations and asks what additional evidence would distinguish between them.

The most defensible next step is therefore publish the method so that another team can replicate it. The report expresses this recommendation directly: It recommends that later observers should publish the method so that another team can replicate it. Its final proposal adds a concrete way of improving the evidence: For a follow-up, the team recommends compare the same indicators with a group that did not receive the intervention. These steps would allow later readers to assess the method rather than relying on the authority of the original authors.

Another issue is transferability. Evidence collected in a university study group cannot automatically be applied to every organisation dealing with business and sustainability. Differences in scale, policy, culture and available support may change both the problem and the most appropriate response.

In practice, the value of the exercise lies in the questions it leaves open. What would happen in another setting? Would the result remain if the support changed? Which groups were not represented? Those questions are not signs of failure; they are the basis for responsible follow-up work.

It is tempting to treat a numerical comparison as if it supplied its own explanation. The project shows why that shortcut is unsafe. The measure, accuracy and confidence, was selected because it could be collected within the available setting, while the method, short structured interviews, defined how the information was gathered. Neither choice removed the effects of attendance, experience or expectations. In work on business and sustainability, such factors may influence both the measured outcome and the decision to participate. The initial observation that the result showed a modest improvement and the later finding that it the second approach was more consistent describe a pattern; they do not establish which factor produced it. For practitioners, the case offers a question to investigate rather than an instruction to copy. A team working in a university study group could first check whether the conditions resemble those in the study and whether accuracy and confidence captures the outcome it cares about. The original evidence came from 33 people observed over 3 weeks; other groups may have different priorities or constraints. Any attempt to apply the finding to business and sustainability should therefore include a review point and an explicit account of uncertainty. The proposed next step, to publish the method so that another team can replicate it, is useful because it tests whether the pattern can be observed beyond the first group.

reading.title: Original Reading Studio · Day 81: Forest Ecology
reading.passage:
Public debate about forest ecology tends to emphasise conclusions. The more difficult work is often methodological: defining a useful measure, selecting a suitable group and deciding what the evidence can reasonably support. A project at a local museum programme used the theme of “Friendly fungi help forests fight climate change” to examine one manageable question: which conditions help people make a more informed choice?

At a local museum programme, the team designed a small investigation around a specific outcome. The factual details are important: The team worked with 40 volunteers over 8 weeks and used direct observation and follow-up questions. The initial investigation used direct observation and follow-up questions as its primary research method. The principal measure was the consistency of decisions. By keeping the measure explicit, the researchers could compare observations, although they could not assume that every participant experienced the process in the same way.

The recorded outcome changed over the course of the project: the initial approach changed very little, while the later review the second approach was more consistent. The authors considered this a meaningful signal, but they resisted treating it as a complete account. A result can identify a question worth pursuing without settling the explanation behind it.

The team warns against treating the report as a final verdict. Its main limitation was that the measures depended partly on self-report. A small or selective sample can reveal useful questions, but it cannot automatically represent a whole community. Additional observations would be needed before the finding could support a broad recommendation.

To make the comparison more informative, the authors added a second-stage programme. The fictional programme at a community learning centre followed 38 participants across 10 review points. It supplied another example of how an outcome might be tracked, but it did not remove the original study’s limitations. A new group can strengthen a line of enquiry only when the method and its differences are reported clearly.

The authors separate the observation from the story that might be told about it. A difference in the forest ecology results is not sufficient to show that the procedure was responsible for the outcome. For instance, a change may coincide with a new procedure while also reflecting a change in participation or external support. The report does not treat timing alone as proof of causation.

Instead of announcing a universal solution, the authors propose a testable next stage. The authors recommend that future work should repeat the project with a broader group. The final recommendation is that researchers should repeat the comparison in two additional settings and publish the measurement procedure This would make the reasoning transparent and help prevent a context-specific result from being treated as a rule for every setting.

This is why a recommendation should identify the conditions under which it is expected to work. In discussions of forest ecology, a general statement may sound persuasive, but it is less useful than a testable proposal with a clear outcome and a transparent method.

For decision-makers, the implication is that evidence should be revisited rather than treated as permanent. A policy can begin with a plausible explanation, but its continuation should depend on transparent measures, feedback from affected groups and a willingness to alter the approach when the results do not support it.

Additional explicit evidence note: For a follow-up, the team recommends repeat the comparison in two additional settings and publish the measurement procedure.

The report’s method should be considered alongside the outcome it records. the consistency of decisions was useful as a consistent indicator, but its meaning depends on how it relates to people’s real circumstances. The team used direct observation and follow-up questions to examine the question in a manageable way. Even so, participants may have interpreted instructions differently, or may have had unequal access to the support needed to complete the task. These possibilities are relevant to any conclusion about forest ecology. The first result changed very little, while the later review the second approach was more consistent. A stronger design would need to examine these alternative explanations directly rather than assuming that the intervention alone produced the observed pattern. The case also raises a question about time. A result observed over 8 weeks may not remain stable after the project ends, particularly if participants receive additional support while the study is active. The team at a local museum programme worked with 40 people, but a longer follow-up could reveal whether the recorded change persists or disappears. Future work on forest ecology should consider both immediate performance and later outcomes. The proposed action, to repeat the project with a broader group, could be strengthened by adding a later review point and describing any changes in participation. This would help distinguish a short-lived response from a more durable effect.

reading.passage:
The practical significance of energy transition depends on the circumstances in which people encounter it. A finding from one institution may not transfer unchanged to another, even when the headline appears similar. Discussion of energy transition often presents two apparently opposing positions. Supporters of a structured approach argue that it makes expectations visible and progress easier to monitor. Critics respond that a rigid 

The project was deliberately limited in scope. It was conducted at a student support office, and the report explains who or what was included and how the evidence was gathered: To compare the arguments, a team at a student support office reviewed 47 learning or work records over 5 weeks. The initial investigation used a controlled comparison of two routines as its primary research method. Its central measure was participants’ ability to transfer the skill. The design prioritised a clear record over a broad claim about every possible context.

The initial evidence showed that the approach improved at first and then levelled off. Following a review, neither approach was clearly superior. This did not eliminate disagreement among participants. Instead, it highlighted the importance of checking whether a procedure is understandable, whether support is available and whether the outcome is measured in a consistent way.

There is an important qualification to the result. The evidence must be interpreted carefully because the sample was self-selected. The researchers therefore avoid claiming that the study has isolated a single cause. Other influences may have shaped the outcome, and those influences would need to be measured before a stronger conclusion could be justified.

The follow-up was intended to test the durability of the observation, not to manufacture a stronger headline. The fictional programme at a regional training programme followed 45 participants across 4 review points. Readers should note that a second sample may differ from the first in experience, access and motivation. Unless those differences are considered, a simple comparison can create an impression of certainty that the evidence does not warrant.

A reader should resist the temptation to turn an association into a causal statement. The recorded pattern in the energy transition case should be interpreted as an association rather than a confirmed causal effect. To test a causal explanation, a later study would need a stronger comparison, clearer records of relevant conditions and a transparent account of missing data.

The team’s conclusion is deliberately conditional. The team suggests that future research should compare more than one setting before making a general claim. The follow-up plan is described as follows: For a follow-up, the team recommends collect evidence over a longer period and report missing observations. A decision should be reviewed when new evidence appears, especially where the consequences fall differently across groups. The report therefore favours a learning process over a one-off declaration.

The case encourages readers to examine the relationship between the chosen measure and the real-world question. A measure of participants’ ability to transfer the skill may be informative, yet it should not be confused with a complete account of wellbeing, quality or long-term success.

The passage therefore asks readers to pay attention to both content and method. A statistic without context can mislead, while a carefully qualified result can still inform a sensible next step. The strongest conclusion is the one that does not claim more than the evidence can bear.

A further issue concerns the difference between consistency and validity. A measure can be recorded in the same way on several occasions without fully representing the underlying issue. In this case, participants’ ability to transfer the skill was sufficiently clear for the investigators to compare observations, and a controlled comparison of two routines gave the team a defined procedure. Nevertheless, the result could still be affected by conditions that were not part of the formal record. This is particularly important when a report on energy transition is used to guide practice. The early pattern improved at first and then levelled off; the later pattern neither approach was clearly superior. Both deserve attention, but neither should be expanded into a claim that exceeds the evidence. The audience for the report matters as much as the result. A decision-maker in a student support office might use the findings to identify a procedure worth reviewing, while another organisation could face different staffing, resources or participant needs. The first sample involved 47 people over 5 weeks; it describes the scope of this exercise, not every group affected by energy transition. A stronger follow-up would preserve the definition of participants’ ability to transfer the skill, explain how participants were selected and record missing observations. It could then test the recommendation to compare more than one setting before making a general claim. Publishing the method and its limitations would let readers judge whether the finding transfers beyond the original setting.

reading.title: Original Reading Studio · Day 83: Nutrition And Measurement
reading.passage:
When policy-makers or educators consider nutrition and measurement, they face a familiar problem: the evidence may point in one direction while the conditions of implementation point in another. A practical investigation of nutrition and measurement can be organised into a sequence rather than treated as one large question.

To avoid relying solely on opinion, the investigators established a procedure at a community learning centre. The report specifies the size and duration of the initial work: 25 participants took part for 10 weeks, while the team used a comparison of several case studies. The initial investigation used a comparison of several case studies as its primary research method. The team monitored the range of strategies used, allowing it to compare the first observations with later ones while keeping the limits of the sample visible.

The report describes a modest but informative pattern. At first, the result varied substantially between participants; subsequently, neither approach was clearly superior. The authors note that the shift should be interpreted in context. An improvement in one measure may coexist with costs or difficulties that the measure does not capture.

The findings are bounded by the quality of the available evidence. The team recorded that the measures depended partly on self-report, so it did not claim to have found a universal solution. This is not a minor technical detail: if the sample or measurement is incomplete, a numerical difference may look more decisive than it really is. Replication and transparent reporting would help readers judge its reliability. The relevant factual statement is also clear: A practical investigation of nutrition and measurement can be organised into a sequence rather than treated as one large question.

The second stage adds a further point of comparison. The fictional programme at a small public-service team followed 52 participants across 7 review points. The figures are included to support reading practice, not to suggest that the programme has been independently evaluated. They allow the reader to examine how sample size, review frequency and measurement choices affect the interpretation of a result.

The numerical account is accompanied by a warning about interpretation. For this study of nutrition and measurement, the outcome may have changed alongside the intervention without being caused by it. This makes the report more cautious, but also more useful: it shows not only what was observed, but also what the observations are unable to prove.

The practical recommendation is to improve the quality of comparison before expanding the intervention. It recommends that the next project should publish the method so that another team can replicate it. The authors add one more research priority: For a follow-up, the team recommends invite an independent team to check the coding rules before drawing a wider conclusion. A transparent record would allow other researchers to check whether the conclusions follow from the evidence.

For anyone evaluating a proposal about nutrition and measurement, the next question is not simply whether the reported result is positive. It is whether the same result would remain under a different comparison, whether the cost of the procedure is acceptable and which groups might experience a different effect.

A responsible interpretation keeps three questions separate: what was observed, what might explain it and what should be tested next. The report is useful precisely because it does not collapse those questions into a single confident statement.

The evidence is strongest when it is read at the scale at which it was collected. The investigation recorded the range of strategies used through a comparison of several case studies, producing a useful account of a limited exercise. It did not provide a complete description of all the social, practical or personal factors connected with nutrition and measurement. Even a carefully recorded change may have several explanations: participants could have learned the procedure, the environment may have changed, or the instructions may have become clearer. The difference between the early result, which varied substantially between participants, and the later result, in which neither approach was clearly superior, therefore identifies an issue for further study rather than a single cause. There is also a question of fairness. An intervention that appears helpful for one group may create extra demands for people with less time, different prior knowledge or limited access to resources. A study involving 25 people at a community learning centre over 10 weeks cannot resolve every such issue. Before adopting the approach in another context, decision-makers should ask whether the same outcome is valued by all affected groups and whether the measure, the range of strategies used, captures unequal effects. The recommendation to publish the method so that another team can replicate it provides a route to examine that question, especially if the next report includes the experiences of people who were not represented in the original sample.

listening.title: In-App Listening · Day 83: Nutrition And Measurement · Case Review
listening.script:
Host: Our topic today is nutrition and measurement, approached through a project review.

Guest: A project record should include more than a headline result. It needs the setting, the method, the sequence of decisions and a note about uncertainty.

Host: We will use those elements to assess the case.

The account was prepared by Professor Ellis. It concerns “Cambridge IELTS 11 Test 4” and describes work carried out at a public information project. The observation period was 6 weeks. The host stresses that this information describes the exercise itself, not a general population.

Host: The initial proposal was a trial with volunteers. Does that mean the project followed it exactly?

Guest: No. The review process matters. The record needs to distinguish the first proposal from the arrangement confirmed after the team considered the practical details.

Today we are looking at nutrition and measurement, using the case titled Cambridge IELTS 11 Test 4.

We began with 43 volunteers and followed the work for 6 weeks.

The final decision was a follow-up interview.

Guest: We will meet on Wednesday at 15:30, then compare the notes with a second group.

Guest: The clearest observation was that a small change improved the clarity of the final explanation.

Host: How should listeners interpret the observation about nutrition and measurement?

Guest: Carefully. The observation describes what happened in this group. It does not, by itself, show that one factor caused the result or that every other group would respond in the same way.

The guest noted that the project record is intended to support discussion, not to serve as a final policy recommendation. Any wider decision would need additional evidence, a larger range of settings and feedback from the people affected. Reporting the limitations is part of the result, not an apology for having them.

Host: What should a second team do before comparing its own work with this case?

Guest: It should keep the same definitions where possible, explain any differences in method and report who was included. If the procedure changes, the comparison needs to say so openly.

Host: Is there anything else that a reader should be careful about when interpreting work on nutrition and measurement?

Guest: Yes. A memorable example can be useful, but it is not a substitute for a wider evidence base. The next stage should test whether the pattern appears under different conditions, and the report should include results that do not fit the first expectation.

That brings the briefing to a close. The project has a clear record and a next step, but its wider significance remains a question for further work. Listeners should keep the factual details separate from their own expectations about what the result might mean.

reading.title: Original Reading Studio · Day 84: Nutrition And Measurement
reading.passage:
Questions about nutrition and measurement are best approached by distinguishing observation from explanation. An apparent improvement can be real without proving which factor produced it. Research into nutrition and measurement can produce findings that appear inconsistent because studies often ask different questions.

The initial phase focused on one setting rather than attempting to represent an entire population. It was carried out at a workplace training unit. The report states: It included 32 participants and lasted 7 weeks. The initial investigation used a questionnaire followed by interviews as its primary research method. The researchers concentrated on the number of completed tasks, a choice that made change easier to describe but did not remove every source of uncertainty.

The team found that the first arrangement produced a clearer result after feedback. Later evidence indicated that the flexible option worked better for some participants. The practical lesson was not that one format should always replace another. It was that decisions should be reviewed against more than one indicator and should remain open to revision when the evidence changes.

The analysis does not hide the main uncertainty. In particular, the sample was self-selected. The authors argue that readers should consider the context before applying the result elsewhere. That approach is more demanding than accepting a headline, but it reduces the risk of turning a limited observation into an unsupported rule.

The authors did not stop at the first set of observations. They added a distinct follow-up: The fictional programme at a university support unit followed 59 participants across 10 review points. The second phase is best understood as a separate case. It invites a comparison of methods and conditions rather than a direct claim that one group performed better than another.

The authors argue that the result should guide the next question rather than end the discussion. The report on nutrition and measurement does not rule out other influences, so the observed difference cannot be attributed to one approach alone. If a different factor explains the change, a policy based on the wrong explanation could waste resources or disadvantage the very group it was intended to support.

The report identifies a next step that can be evaluated rather than merely announced. The most useful next step is to repeat the project with a broader group. It then proposes a more detailed follow-up: For a follow-up, the team recommends compare the same indicators with a group that did not receive the intervention. If the next study reports its limits and measures consistently, readers will be better placed to judge whether its findings apply beyond the original context.

The passage also shows that a practical decision can remain provisional. A team may act on the best available evidence while still recording uncertainty, setting a review point and agreeing in advance what new information would lead it to change course.

Ultimately, the exercise rewards careful reading rather than the memorisation of a headline. The reader must connect a claim to its evidence, recognise the limits of the sample and understand why a follow-up design matters. Those habits transfer to academic texts well beyond this topic.

The investigators’ choices reveal both the value and the limit of operational definitions. By defining the number of completed tasks, they made one part of nutrition and measurement observable; by adopting a questionnaire followed by interviews, they established how that observation would be collected. Yet operational clarity does not make a measure exhaustive. It remains possible that a different indicator would produce a different assessment of the same situation. The early observations showed that the result produced a clearer result after feedback, while the later review found that it the flexible option worked better for some participants. Such a contrast can guide a more precise enquiry, provided that the next study states what it is measuring and what remains outside its scope. Another organisation should resist importing the result without checking local conditions. The same procedure may work differently where staff have less time, where materials are harder to obtain or where participants have different experience. The original project took place at a workplace training unit, included 32 people and lasted 7 weeks. A transfer study on nutrition and measurement should make those differences visible, while keeping the central measure stable enough to permit comparison. Testing the recommendation to repeat the project with a broader group would provide a structured way to do this. Reporting both successful and inconclusive outcomes would be important; otherwise, later readers would see only evidence that supports the initial view.

listening.script:
Host: Welcome to the study discussion. We are considering nutrition and measurement and how a modest investigation can be interpreted.

Guest: The case is useful for practising careful listening because it contains a revised plan, a measured observation and a future appointment.

Host: Listen for the final confirmed details rather than the first suggestion.

In introducing the case, the host identifies “Weekly Reading consolidation”. The guest, Aisha Rahman, worked with the project at a workplace training unit. Its recorded period was 2 weeks, which gives the team a limited but usable basis for reviewing the sequence.

Host: Could you explain how the team moved from an open discussion to a final arrangement?

Guest: The decision was made after the first review. That is why the final wording in the project record is important for an accurate summary.

Today we are looking at nutrition and measurement, using the case titled Weekly Reading consolidation.

We began with 54 volunteers and followed the work for 2 weeks.

The final decision was a second trial in another group.

Guest: We will meet on Friday at 10:30, then compare the notes with a second group.

Guest: The clearest observation was that the group needed more time than expected to compare the options.

Host: How should listeners interpret the observation about nutrition and measurement?

Guest: Carefully. The observation describes what happened in this group. It does not, by itself, show that one factor caused the result or that every other group would respond in the same way.

During the review, the team compared the original proposal with what had actually been completed. The first idea was discussed, but it was not treated as a final decision. This is a common feature of project work: a practical arrangement may change once the team sees the available evidence, staffing requirements or feedback from participants.

Host: What should a second team do before comparing its own work with this case?

Guest: It should keep the same definitions where possible, explain any differences in method and report who was included. If the procedure changes, the comparison needs to say so openly.

Host: Is there anything else that a reader should be careful about when interpreting work on nutrition and measurement?

Guest: Yes. A memorable example can be useful, but it is not a substitute for a wider evidence base. The next stage should test whether the pattern appears under different conditions, and the report should include results that do not fit the first expectation.

The speakers agree that transparent reporting is more valuable than an overconfident headline. The team will keep the original record, describe any new procedure and explain what can reasonably be concluded. That is the standard they intend to use when the next group is reviewed.

stage27.name: Writing Expert Studio

weekly_source_packs.theme: Urban life, public space and liveability
weekly_source_packs.purpose: Task 2 idea-building: compare growth, access, health and environmental trade-offs.

sources.name: National Geographic · Urban heat island solutions
sources.use: Find one claim, one practical response and one limitation; paraphrase rather than copy.

sources.name: Our World in Data · Urbanization
sources.use: Check how urbanisation is defined; distinguish population share from city growth.

weekly_source_packs.output: Write a balanced paragraph on whether city investment should prioritise transport, green space or housing. Include a counterpoint.

weekly_source_packs.purpose: Argument quality: separate correlation from causation and evaluate competing claims.

sources.name: The Guardian · Screen use and children’s learning (reported debate)
sources.use: Identify the claim and the qualifications raised by other education experts; do not treat a reported opinion as settled fact.

sources.name: Cambridge English · Write & Improve
sources.use: Submit your own short paragraph, review the tool’s feedback, then edit it yourself. It is not an IELTS band score.

weekly_source_packs.output: Write a Task 2 body paragraph that weighs educational benefits against distraction and access differences.

weekly_source_packs.theme: Energy use and the transition to low-carbon systems
weekly_source_packs.purpose: Evidence handling: understand units, time series, shares and per-person comparisons.

sources.name: Our World in Data · Energy
sources.use: Check whether a chart measures primary energy, electricity generation or final consumption; these are not interchangeable.

sources.name: Our World in Data · Energy mix
sources.use: Describe the largest sources and changes; note the metric and data source before making a comparison.

weekly_source_packs.output: Write a Task 1-style overview from an independently selected public chart, recording the chart title, metric, date range and source.

weekly_source_packs.purpose: Compare places and indicators without confusing absolute totals with percentages.

sources.name: World Bank Data · Urban Development
sources.use: Select one indicator and note its unit, year, country coverage and limitations.

sources.name: Our World in Data · Urbanization
sources.use: Compare the measure used and explain what it does not measure.

weekly_source_packs.output: Create a four-sentence comparison plan: highest, lowest, notable gap and one careful limitation.

weekly_source_packs.purpose: Use data cautiously and avoid claims beyond the indicator.

sources.name: Our World in Data · Average years of schooling
sources.use: Check the age group, date and the fact that years of schooling do not directly measure learning quality.

sources.name: The Guardian · Education topic
sources.use: Compare an editorial claim with data or research before using it as an example.

weekly_source_packs.output: Write a Task 2 paragraph about education investment that distinguishes access, attainment and learning quality.

weekly_source_packs.purpose: Build a precise cause–effect chain and evaluate proposed solutions.

sources.name: National Geographic · Extreme heat days in US cities
sources.kind: journalism based on an external analysis
sources.use: Identify the time comparison and the population/geographic scope; do not generalise beyond it.

sources.name: Our World in Data · CO₂ and greenhouse gas emissions
sources.use: Differentiate territorial emissions, consumption-based emissions and per-capita measures.

weekly_source_packs.output: Build a causes → consequences → response plan and include one limitation or unintended consequence.

weekly_source_packs.purpose: Develop a qualified position rather than a one-sided technology argument.

sources.name: The Guardian · Technology and education
sources.use: Choose a current article, record its publication date and separate reported facts from opinion.

sources.name: Cambridge English · Learning English resources
sources.use: Select a B2/C1 writing or language activity and record which correction you applied.

weekly_source_packs.output: Write a nuanced thesis on AI and work, then develop a benefit, a risk and a condition under which the benefit is more likely.

weekly_source_packs.purpose: Practise systems thinking and careful cause/effect explanation.

sources.name: Our World in Data · Clean water and sanitation
sources.use: Check whether the indicator measures safely managed water, basic access or sanitation; these are not interchangeable.

sources.name: WHO · Drinking-water
sources.use: Use the factsheet to understand terms and consequences; paraphrase and cite the organisation.

weekly_source_packs.output: Write a problem–solution outline with a feasible intervention, responsible actor and measurable outcome.

weekly_source_packs.purpose: Compare consumer choice, policy and supply-side factors.

sources.name: National Geographic · Environment
sources.use: Choose one food/environment feature; identify the claim, evidence and caveat.

sources.name: Our World in Data · Food
sources.use: Check whether the measure is food supply, consumption, production or waste.

weekly_source_packs.output: Write a two-sided argument about sustainable food choices, including what individual action cannot solve alone.

weekly_source_packs.purpose: Use measured outcomes accurately and avoid unsupported medical generalisations.

sources.name: WHO · Health topics
sources.use: Use as background for definitions and public-health context; do not present a broad topic page as a specific study.

sources.name: The Guardian · Health
sources.use: Record article date, named source and any uncertainty or disagreement.

weekly_source_packs.output: Develop a policy paragraph that explains who benefits, who pays and what evidence would show success.

weekly_source_packs.purpose: Build complex comparisons and acknowledge competing land-use priorities.

sources.name: National Geographic · Environment
sources.use: Choose a biodiversity or conservation article and separate observation from proposed solution.

sources.name: Our World in Data · Biodiversity
sources.use: Check which biodiversity measure is shown and what its geographical scope means.

weekly_source_packs.output: Write a balanced paragraph on conservation and development, including a practical trade-off and a reasoned solution.

weekly_source_packs.theme: Final synthesis and IELTS examiner expectations
weekly_source_packs.purpose: Compare your work with official samples, descriptor language and authentic feedback.

sources.name: IELTS.org · Academic Writing sample tasks and examiner comments
sources.use: Review the sample task and examiner comments; compare organisation and task coverage, not memorised phrases.

sources.name: IELTS.org · Writing assessment resources
sources.use: Read the four criteria and annotate exact evidence in your own response.

sources.name: British Council · Academic Writing practice
sources.use: Complete an official sample and compare your response with the published examiner guidance where available.

weekly_source_packs.output: Complete a final Task 1 + Task 2 pair, then compare both drafts with the relevant criterion checklist.

original_model_responses.title: Model: a changing indicator over four years
original_model_responses.prompt: The line graph shows a fictional indicator in 2010, 2015, 2020 and 2025.
original_model_responses.response:
The line graph illustrates changes in a fictional indicator between 2010 and 2025. Overall, the figure fluctuated considerably, reaching a clear peak in 2020 before falling to its lowest level at the end of the period.

The indicator began at 57 points in 2010, then declined to 45 in 2015. It subsequently rose sharply by 38 points to a high of 83 in 2020. This upward movement was not sustained, however. By 2025, the figure had dropped to 28 points, which was less than half the opening value.

The most notable feature is therefore the contrast between the temporary peak in 2020 and the substantial decline over the final five years. Across the whole period, the indicator fell by 29 points, despite the marked mid-period recovery. The data describe a pattern of fluctuation rather than a steady upward or downward trend. In particular, the 2020 peak should not be presented as evidence of a long-term increase, because the final observation is markedly lower than that peak.
original_model_responses.annotation: The overview identifies the main pattern first; the body selects the peak, lowest point, turning point and net change. No cause is invented.

original_model_responses.title: Model: four programme stages
original_model_responses.prompt: The bar chart compares four fictional programme stages.
original_model_responses.response:
The bar chart compares the number of reported cases at four stages of a fictional programme. Overall, the figure increased sharply after the initial stage, reached its highest point at the follow-up, and then declined slightly in the final review.

At the outset, 19 cases were recorded. This was substantially lower than the figure after the adjustment, which rose to 85. The number then increased marginally to 87 at the follow-up stage, representing the peak of the period. In the final review, the total fell to 76, a reduction of 11 cases compared with the preceding stage.

Despite the small decrease at the end, the final figure remained approximately four times as high as the initial value. The main feature is the rapid rise between the first and second stages, followed by relative stability at a much higher level. The figures do not indicate why the change occurred; they only show how the recorded totals differed across the four stages.
original_model_responses.annotation: The comparison is selective and the final sentence avoids causal speculation.

original_model_responses.title: Model: distribution of four response categories
original_model_responses.prompt: The pie chart shows the fictional distribution of four response categories.
original_model_responses.response:
The pie chart illustrates how responses were distributed across four fictional categories. Overall, the primary category accounted for the largest share, while the alternative category represented the smallest proportion. Together, the two largest categories made up almost two thirds of all responses.

The primary category was the most common, at 35%. The secondary category followed closely, accounting for 30%, which was five percentage points lower. By contrast, the alternative category represented only 14% of responses, making it the smallest segment. The remaining category accounted for 21%.

The difference between the largest and smallest shares was 21 percentage points. It is also notable that the two leading categories together represented 65% of the total, whereas the other two accounted for the remaining 35%. These proportions show that responses were concentrated in the first two categories rather than being evenly distributed. A useful final check is to confirm that the four percentages sum to 100%, and to use percentage-point language when comparing the size of two shares.
original_model_responses.annotation: Percentages are calculated from the fictional dataset. “Percentage points” is used for the difference between shares.

original_model_responses.title: Model: comparison across four groups
original_model_responses.prompt: The table presents fictional results for four comparison groups.
original_model_responses.response:
The table compares the number of units recorded in four fictional groups. Overall, Group C had the highest figure, whereas Group A recorded the lowest. Groups B and D occupied the middle positions, although the difference between them was relatively small.

Group C recorded 70 units, compared with 36 in Group A, a gap of 34. Group B was next, at 60 units, while Group D recorded 32. The two middle groups therefore differed by 28 units, so they were not as close as their positions in the ranking might initially suggest.

The most notable feature is the contrast between Group C and Group A. Group C’s total was almost twice that of Group A, while the figures for Groups B and D fell between these extremes. A concise report should focus on the ranking and the largest gap rather than describe every cell at equal length. All figures are illustrative practice data and should be reported only in the unit stated by the table.
original_model_responses.annotation: The model ranks the groups and highlights the largest gap; all figures match the displayed example dataset.

original_model_responses.title: Model: a six-stage cataloguing process
original_model_responses.prompt: The diagram illustrates six stages in a cataloguing process.
original_model_responses.response:
The diagram illustrates how an object is catalogued, from its collection to the publication of an approved record. Overall, the procedure consists of six stages and follows a linear sequence, with checks carried out before the final record is made public.

First, objects are collected from the storage room and given temporary identification labels. Their condition is then photographed from several angles. Once this visual record has been created, the catalogue entry is checked against the physical object to ensure that the information is consistent.

In the next stage, a specialist examines any descriptions that remain uncertain. Finally, after the record has been approved, it is added to the public archive. The process therefore moves from initial identification and documentation to verification, specialist review and publication. No decision or cause beyond the stages shown in the diagram is assumed. The report also avoids describing the specialist review as an approval stage until the diagram explicitly shows that the record has been approved, which occurs immediately before publication.
original_model_responses.annotation: The process is written in a logical sequence, using passive forms and no invented stages.

original_model_responses.title: Model: a site before and after redevelopment
original_model_responses.prompt: The maps show a fictional site before and after redevelopment.
original_model_responses.response:
The maps compare a fictional site before and after redevelopment. Overall, the layout was modernised: the main gallery was expanded, the courtyard became a covered learning area, and the former storage building was replaced by a conservation studio. The north gate was retained but improved with an access ramp.

Before redevelopment, the site contained a north gate, a main gallery, a small courtyard and a storage building. In the later plan, the entrance remained in the same general position, although an access ramp was added. The gallery occupied a larger area than before, while the courtyard was converted into a covered space for learning.

The most substantial change was the replacement of the storage building with a new conservation studio. Taken together, the changes increased the range of facilities while retaining the main entrance and gallery as recognisable features. As the plans are schematic, the description focuses on named features rather than distances or exact areas.
original_model_responses.annotation: The overview names the most important changes, and the report does not invent scale, direction or measurements.

original_model_responses.title: Model: public investment and long-term benefits
original_model_responses.prompt: Some people believe that governments should invest more in preventive public services. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
original_model_responses.response:
Public investment in preventive services is often less visible than spending on immediate problems, yet it can produce substantial benefits over time. I largely agree that governments should give prevention a higher priority, provided that essential treatment and emergency provision are not weakened.

The strongest argument for prevention is that early intervention can reduce the scale and cost of later difficulties. When communities have reliable access to clear information, screening and practical support, problems may be identified before they become more complex. This can improve individual outcomes while reducing pressure on public institutions. Prevention can also make services fairer, since people with fewer resources are often least able to pay for early support themselves.

However, prevention should not be treated as a substitute for immediate care. Some needs are urgent, and public systems must retain enough capacity to respond to illness, accidents and unexpected demand. In addition, preventive programmes are only effective when they are accessible and supported by credible evidence. A poorly designed campaign may consume resources without changing behaviour.

The most effective policy is therefore a balanced one: maintain dependable emergency services while directing additional investment towards preventive measures whose outcomes can be evaluated. This approach recognises both the long-term value of prevention and the continuing importance of immediate support. It also allows decision-makers to compare the cost of a programme with measurable outcomes, rather than assuming that every preventive intervention is automatically effective. Public reporting should also show who benefits, how widely the service is used and whether outcomes differ between neighbourhoods. Such evidence makes it easier to improve a programme and explain why its funding should continue.
original_model_responses.annotation: A clear but qualified position is maintained; each body paragraph develops a distinct reason and acknowledges limits.

original_model_responses.title: Model: individual responsibility and institutional action
original_model_responses.prompt: Some people think individuals are mainly responsible for improving public wellbeing, while others believe institutions should take the lead. Discuss both views and give your opinion.
original_model_responses.response:
People disagree about whether public wellbeing depends primarily on personal choices or on the institutions that shape everyday life. Although individuals must take responsibility for their own decisions, I believe that institutions have the greater ability to create conditions in which positive choices are realistic and widely available.

Those who emphasise individual responsibility argue that lasting change requires personal commitment. People decide what habits to adopt, whether to seek reliable information and how consistently to follow advice. Even well-funded public programmes may have little effect if individuals do not engage with them. Personal responsibility also matters because needs and circumstances differ, making a single policy unsuitable for everyone.

Nevertheless, institutions influence the options available to the public. Schools, employers and local authorities can provide safe spaces, accessible information and services that individuals cannot create on their own. For example, a person may understand the value of regular activity but lack safe public areas or affordable facilities. In such circumstances, advice alone is unlikely to solve the problem. Institutional decisions can therefore affect entire communities, including people with limited resources.

In my view, the two forms of responsibility are complementary, but institutional action should lead. Public bodies can establish fair conditions, while individuals decide how to use the opportunities provided. A policy is most effective when it combines accessible services with informed personal participation. This division of responsibility avoids blaming individuals for barriers they cannot remove themselves, while still recognising that public programmes depend on engagement and trust. It is therefore more realistic to ask institutions to create fair opportunities and residents to participate in ways that suit their circumstances.
original_model_responses.annotation: Both views receive development before the writer gives a reasoned judgement.

original_model_responses.title: Model: advantages and disadvantages of digital services
original_model_responses.prompt: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of the growing use of digital public services.
original_model_responses.response:
Digital public services can make everyday administration faster and more convenient, but their expansion also raises questions about access and reliability. On balance, the advantages are considerable, although they depend on whether non-digital alternatives remain available.

One clear benefit is efficiency. People may complete routine tasks without travelling to an office or waiting for an appointment. This can save time for users and allow public employees to focus on cases that require direct attention. Digital systems can also make information easier to update and distribute, reducing the risk that different offices provide inconsistent instructions.

However, online services may exclude people who lack reliable internet access, suitable devices or confidence using digital tools. Technical failures can also interrupt essential services, while poorly protected systems create privacy and security risks. These disadvantages are particularly serious when a digital platform becomes the only route to support.

The benefits therefore outweigh the drawbacks only when services are designed inclusively. In addition, digital systems should be introduced gradually, with clear instructions and accessible support, so that people who are less confident with technology are not left behind during the transition. Clear complaints procedures are also necessary for users who encounter errors. Governments should provide accessible interfaces, protect personal data and retain telephone or face-to-face help for those who need it. Digital delivery should improve access rather than make assistance conditional on technical ability. Regular user testing, clear privacy rules and staff support are therefore as important as the software itself; otherwise, a system designed for efficiency may create new forms of exclusion.
original_model_responses.annotation: The essay compares both sides and makes the judgement conditional, not absolute.

original_model_responses.title: Model: congestion and practical measures
original_model_responses.prompt: Many cities face increasing traffic congestion. What problems does this cause, and what measures could address it?
original_model_responses.response:
Growing traffic congestion creates problems that extend beyond longer journeys. It affects the environment, reduces economic efficiency and can make urban life less predictable. Addressing it requires more than simply building additional roads; cities need reliable alternatives to private car use.

One consequence is the loss of time. When roads are heavily congested, workers and businesses cannot plan journeys accurately, and deliveries become less dependable. Traffic also increases local air pollution and noise, which can reduce residents’ quality of life. These effects are not distributed equally: people living near major roads may experience the greatest exposure, even if they do not own a car.

A practical response is to improve the frequency, coverage and affordability of public transport. If buses and trains provide dependable connections, some commuters may choose them instead of driving. Safe walking and cycling routes can also make short journeys less car-dependent. In the busiest areas, carefully designed parking policies or congestion charges may encourage a shift, although such measures should be accompanied by affordable alternatives so that lower-income residents are not unfairly burdened.

No single measure will remove congestion entirely. A combination of better public transport, safer active travel and fair demand management is more likely to reduce traffic while preserving access to jobs and services. The effectiveness of each measure should be assessed through journey reliability, affordability and local air-quality indicators, rather than road speed alone. Reviews should be published so residents can judge whether the chosen measures improve journey reliability and access, rather than merely shifting traffic from one street to another. This is especially important when new charges affect people who have few alternatives.
original_model_responses.annotation: The response links each proposed solution to a problem and notes an equity risk.

original_model_responses.title: Model: why a trend is growing and what it may mean
original_model_responses.prompt: More people are choosing to study online. Why is this happening, and what effects may it have on education?
original_model_responses.response:
Online study has become more common because digital platforms offer flexibility and can connect learners with courses that may not be available locally. This shift can widen access, but it may also change the way students participate and receive support.

A major reason for the growth of online learning is convenience. Learners can often choose when to study and avoid the cost or time associated with travelling to an educational institution. Online platforms may also provide access to specialist teachers, recorded explanations and materials that can be revisited. For adults who combine education with work or family responsibilities, this flexibility can make further study possible.

The effects are mixed. On the positive side, students can learn at a pace that suits their needs and may benefit from a wider range of resources. However, online education can reduce informal interaction with teachers and classmates. Learners who have limited internet access, unsuitable study conditions or weak self-management skills may find it difficult to remain engaged. The quality of online courses also varies, so access to a platform does not automatically guarantee effective learning.

Overall, online study is likely to remain an important part of education because it offers genuine flexibility. Its value will depend on course design, student support and whether institutions provide alternatives for learners who cannot study effectively online. A blended model may therefore be preferable in subjects that require discussion, practical feedback or supervised work, while fully online provision can remain useful for flexible content-based study. Teachers can review these supports as learners become more confident, gradually reducing guidance while keeping help available when a student encounters a new difficulty.
original_model_responses.annotation: Both parts of the question are answered in separate, developed sections.

stage27.pedagogy: Task-focused Academic Writing practice. Official exam descriptors inform the learning checklist; local checks are heuristic and never claim to assign an IELTS band.
stage27.data_policy: All 84 in-app Task 1 datasets are original fictional practice datasets. Real-world reading and data sources are linked separately for idea-building and evidence literacy; figures are not copied or represented as real statistics.
stage27.rights_policy: No copyrighted publisher tests, paid book scans, protected audio, model scripts or password-protected companion files are bundled. The platform links to official sources and supports the learner’s own licensed study copies.
stage27.language_policy: Uzbek for navigation, explanations and study instructions; English for IELTS prompts, source material, model responses and writing output.
stage27.scoring_policy: Internal criterion review uses four 0–10 practice ratings. Task 2 is weighted twice as much as Task 1 for the combined practice index. This is not an official IELTS band score.
stage27.limitations: Local writing audit is rule-based. It cannot fully evaluate relevance, argument validity, factual accuracy, naturalness or assign an official examiner band.

listeningProtocol.name: Ma’rifat Jamal Listening Cycle
listeningProtocol.status: IELTS Boost learning protocol; synthetic practice audio must not be labelled as authentic IELTS audio.
listeningProtocol.purpose: Sen belgilagan 20 daqiqalik shaxsiy listening protokoli: avval transcriptni yashirib umumiy mazmunni tinglash, xotiradan eslash, chunk dictation, transcript bilan solishtirib xatoni tuzatish va yangi segmentda retest.

steps.name: Blind listen — gist first
steps.task: Transcriptni yopiq qoldir. Audioni bir marta tinglab, faqat mavzu, asosiy fikr va speaker maqsadini yoz. Har bir so‘zni ushlashga urinma.

steps.name: Closed-book recall
steps.task: Audio tugagach transcriptni ochma. Xotiradan 3 ta asosiy fikr, 2 ta muhim detal va eshitilgan bog‘lanishlarni yoz.

steps.name: Chunk dictation
steps.task: Audiodan 3–5 qisqa chunk tanla. Har birini qayta tinglab aynan yoz: articles, endings, plural, prepositions, linking, names va numbers. Transcript hali yopiq qolsin.

steps.name: Transcript audit + repair
steps.task: Endi transcriptni ochib, yozganing bilan so‘zma-so‘z taqqosla. Omission, substitution, spelling, sound-linking, grammar ending, number/name xatolarini belgilab, to‘g‘ri shaklini yoz.

steps.name: Replay + transfer retest
steps.task: Zaif chunklarni yana tingla; bir marta transcript bilan, keyin transcriptsiz qayta yoz. So‘ng boshqa yangi segmentda shu listening ko‘nikmasini sinab ko‘r va 1–3 ta xatoni SRS/Error Log’ga qo‘sh.

scoring.note: Bu 1–10 o‘quv sifati ko‘rsatkichiga yordam beradigan ichki mashq balli; IELTS band score emas.

source_guidance: Primary daily listening is the original IELTS Boost in-app podcast-style script for the selected day; the browser reads it using speech synthesis. This is synthetic practice audio, not an authentic podcast or IELTS recording.
Optional supplement: British Council LearnEnglish Audio Zone is designed for B2/C1 learners and provides audio, transcripts and interactive exercises (availability varies by item).
Optional supplement: TED Talks Daily is an official TED podcast. Use the individual TED talk page for a transcript where available.
Official IELTS Listening sample tasks and recordings are for occasional exam-format calibration; do not redistribute copyrighted recordings or transcripts.
listeningProtocol.transcript_caveat: YouTube auto-generated captions may contain errors. Prefer human-verified transcript where available; record whether transcript was human-made or auto-generated. The app cannot automatically fetch private/external YouTube subtitles, so learner pastes transcript or opens source transcript page.
listeningProtocol.user_definition: Ma’rifat Jamal Listening Cycle — sen nomlagan shaxsiy o‘quv protokoli. U rasmiy IELTS usuli yoki mustaqil validatsiyadan o‘tgan brend sifatida ko‘rsatilmaydi.

quality_disclosure.reading: 84 original hypothetical practice passages; 840 unique questions. 812 have exact passage evidence and 28 are explicit NOT GIVEN absence cases; no official IELTS/Cambridge passage is reproduced.
quality_disclosure.listening: 84 original synthetic MP3 practice recordings; 420 questions. 420/420 question evidence strings exactly match the source script. These are not official or human-recorded IELTS recordings.
quality_disclosure.writing: 84 unique Task 2 prompts; 84 Task 1 visuals across six visual families (14 each). Stage35 adds Task1/Task2-specific criterion anchors and evidence-based learner self-review; not examiner scoring.
quality_disclosure.speaking: 84 original cue cards and 252 Part1 / 252 Part3 prompts. Power Lab review uses four official criterion names, audio replay and transcript evidence. Pronunciation is not inferred from transcript.
quality_disclosure.vocabulary: 19000 unique indexed forms; 677 bundled full glossary entries; 4000 pronunciation-index-only entries; 14323 manual enrichment rows without English definitions. Local source-backed curation is learner-reviewed, not automatically certified.
quality_disclosure.offline: PWA shell can be cached after first HTTPS/localhost load; progress uses local browser storage with temporary-memory fallback in restricted contexts. No cloud sync. Actual device/PWA offline acceptance remains open.
quality_disclosure.games: The learner-facing Game Arena is consolidated to 10 major learning modules. Each module offers 10 practice modes, while the four core studios use that day’s real in-app passage, scripted MP3, Task 1 visual and Speaking prompt.

stage25.name: Advanced Reading Reconstruction
stage25.policy: Daily case passages are clearly labelled original hypothetical practice; weekly source companions are independent syntheses linked to authoritative source pages. No publisher article/test has been reproduced.
stage25.daily_format_jump: Each format card links to the nearest relevant interactive question in the daily comprehension set; formats not present in that day are labelled as a related focus rather than a separate scored item.

stage26.name: Authentic Listening Lab
stage26.score_policy: The 0–10 Listening quality score requires a confirmed source recording, source tasks, transcript audit, written evidence, a transfer retest, all five personal-protocol steps, and explicit self-selected rubric scores. Game challenge points remain separate.
stage26.source_playback_policy: Official external source pages open in a new tab; user-owned licensed audio can be uploaded to the in-app player. No protected audio or transcript is bundled.
stage26.limitations: External player playback and device microphone/audio capabilities remain device-specific and were not verified in this sandbox.
