original_model_responses.title: Model: a changing indicator over four years
original_model_responses.prompt: The line graph shows a fictional indicator in 2010, 2015, 2020 and 2025.
original_model_responses.response:
The line graph illustrates changes in a fictional indicator between 2010 and 2025. Overall, the figure fluctuated considerably, reaching a clear peak in 2020 before falling to its lowest level at the end of the period.

The indicator began at 57 points in 2010, then declined to 45 in 2015. It subsequently rose sharply by 38 points to a high of 83 in 2020. This upward movement was not sustained, however. By 2025, the figure had dropped to 28 points, which was less than half the opening value.

The most notable feature is therefore the contrast between the temporary peak in 2020 and the substantial decline over the final five years. Across the whole period, the indicator fell by 29 points, despite the marked mid-period recovery. The data describe a pattern of fluctuation rather than a steady upward or downward trend. In particular, the 2020 peak should not be presented as evidence of a long-term increase, because the final observation is markedly lower than that peak.
original_model_responses.annotation: The overview identifies the main pattern first; the body selects the peak, lowest point, turning point and net change. No cause is invented.

original_model_responses.title: Model: four programme stages
original_model_responses.prompt: The bar chart compares four fictional programme stages.
original_model_responses.response:
The bar chart compares the number of reported cases at four stages of a fictional programme. Overall, the figure increased sharply after the initial stage, reached its highest point at the follow-up, and then declined slightly in the final review.

At the outset, 19 cases were recorded. This was substantially lower than the figure after the adjustment, which rose to 85. The number then increased marginally to 87 at the follow-up stage, representing the peak of the period. In the final review, the total fell to 76, a reduction of 11 cases compared with the preceding stage.

Despite the small decrease at the end, the final figure remained approximately four times as high as the initial value. The main feature is the rapid rise between the first and second stages, followed by relative stability at a much higher level. The figures do not indicate why the change occurred; they only show how the recorded totals differed across the four stages.
original_model_responses.annotation: The comparison is selective and the final sentence avoids causal speculation.

original_model_responses.title: Model: distribution of four response categories
original_model_responses.prompt: The pie chart shows the fictional distribution of four response categories.
original_model_responses.response:
The pie chart illustrates how responses were distributed across four fictional categories. Overall, the primary category accounted for the largest share, while the alternative category represented the smallest proportion. Together, the two largest categories made up almost two thirds of all responses.

The primary category was the most common, at 35%. The secondary category followed closely, accounting for 30%, which was five percentage points lower. By contrast, the alternative category represented only 14% of responses, making it the smallest segment. The remaining category accounted for 21%.

The difference between the largest and smallest shares was 21 percentage points. It is also notable that the two leading categories together represented 65% of the total, whereas the other two accounted for the remaining 35%. These proportions show that responses were concentrated in the first two categories rather than being evenly distributed. A useful final check is to confirm that the four percentages sum to 100%, and to use percentage-point language when comparing the size of two shares.
original_model_responses.annotation: Percentages are calculated from the fictional dataset. “Percentage points” is used for the difference between shares.

original_model_responses.title: Model: comparison across four groups
original_model_responses.prompt: The table presents fictional results for four comparison groups.
original_model_responses.response:
The table compares the number of units recorded in four fictional groups. Overall, Group C had the highest figure, whereas Group A recorded the lowest. Groups B and D occupied the middle positions, although the difference between them was relatively small.

Group C recorded 70 units, compared with 36 in Group A, a gap of 34. Group B was next, at 60 units, while Group D recorded 32. The two middle groups therefore differed by 28 units, so they were not as close as their positions in the ranking might initially suggest.

The most notable feature is the contrast between Group C and Group A. Group C’s total was almost twice that of Group A, while the figures for Groups B and D fell between these extremes. A concise report should focus on the ranking and the largest gap rather than describe every cell at equal length. All figures are illustrative practice data and should be reported only in the unit stated by the table.
original_model_responses.annotation: The model ranks the groups and highlights the largest gap; all figures match the displayed example dataset.

original_model_responses.title: Model: a six-stage cataloguing process
original_model_responses.prompt: The diagram illustrates six stages in a cataloguing process.
original_model_responses.response:
The diagram illustrates how an object is catalogued, from its collection to the publication of an approved record. Overall, the procedure consists of six stages and follows a linear sequence, with checks carried out before the final record is made public.

First, objects are collected from the storage room and given temporary identification labels. Their condition is then photographed from several angles. Once this visual record has been created, the catalogue entry is checked against the physical object to ensure that the information is consistent.

In the next stage, a specialist examines any descriptions that remain uncertain. Finally, after the record has been approved, it is added to the public archive. The process therefore moves from initial identification and documentation to verification, specialist review and publication. No decision or cause beyond the stages shown in the diagram is assumed. The report also avoids describing the specialist review as an approval stage until the diagram explicitly shows that the record has been approved, which occurs immediately before publication.
original_model_responses.annotation: The process is written in a logical sequence, using passive forms and no invented stages.

original_model_responses.title: Model: a site before and after redevelopment
original_model_responses.prompt: The maps show a fictional site before and after redevelopment.
original_model_responses.response:
The maps compare a fictional site before and after redevelopment. Overall, the layout was modernised: the main gallery was expanded, the courtyard became a covered learning area, and the former storage building was replaced by a conservation studio. The north gate was retained but improved with an access ramp.

Before redevelopment, the site contained a north gate, a main gallery, a small courtyard and a storage building. In the later plan, the entrance remained in the same general position, although an access ramp was added. The gallery occupied a larger area than before, while the courtyard was converted into a covered space for learning.

The most substantial change was the replacement of the storage building with a new conservation studio. Taken together, the changes increased the range of facilities while retaining the main entrance and gallery as recognisable features. As the plans are schematic, the description focuses on named features rather than distances or exact areas.
original_model_responses.annotation: The overview names the most important changes, and the report does not invent scale, direction or measurements.

original_model_responses.title: Model: public investment and long-term benefits
original_model_responses.prompt: Some people believe that governments should invest more in preventive public services. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
original_model_responses.response:
Public investment in preventive services is often less visible than spending on immediate problems, yet it can produce substantial benefits over time. I largely agree that governments should give prevention a higher priority, provided that essential treatment and emergency provision are not weakened.

The strongest argument for prevention is that early intervention can reduce the scale and cost of later difficulties. When communities have reliable access to clear information, screening and practical support, problems may be identified before they become more complex. This can improve individual outcomes while reducing pressure on public institutions. Prevention can also make services fairer, since people with fewer resources are often least able to pay for early support themselves.

However, prevention should not be treated as a substitute for immediate care. Some needs are urgent, and public systems must retain enough capacity to respond to illness, accidents and unexpected demand. In addition, preventive programmes are only effective when they are accessible and supported by credible evidence. A poorly designed campaign may consume resources without changing behaviour.

The most effective policy is therefore a balanced one: maintain dependable emergency services while directing additional investment towards preventive measures whose outcomes can be evaluated. This approach recognises both the long-term value of prevention and the continuing importance of immediate support. It also allows decision-makers to compare the cost of a programme with measurable outcomes, rather than assuming that every preventive intervention is automatically effective. Public reporting should also show who benefits, how widely the service is used and whether outcomes differ between neighbourhoods. Such evidence makes it easier to improve a programme and explain why its funding should continue.
original_model_responses.annotation: A clear but qualified position is maintained; each body paragraph develops a distinct reason and acknowledges limits.

original_model_responses.title: Model: individual responsibility and institutional action
original_model_responses.prompt: Some people think individuals are mainly responsible for improving public wellbeing, while others believe institutions should take the lead. Discuss both views and give your opinion.
original_model_responses.response:
People disagree about whether public wellbeing depends primarily on personal choices or on the institutions that shape everyday life. Although individuals must take responsibility for their own decisions, I believe that institutions have the greater ability to create conditions in which positive choices are realistic and widely available.

Those who emphasise individual responsibility argue that lasting change requires personal commitment. People decide what habits to adopt, whether to seek reliable information and how consistently to follow advice. Even well-funded public programmes may have little effect if individuals do not engage with them. Personal responsibility also matters because needs and circumstances differ, making a single policy unsuitable for everyone.

Nevertheless, institutions influence the options available to the public. Schools, employers and local authorities can provide safe spaces, accessible information and services that individuals cannot create on their own. For example, a person may understand the value of regular activity but lack safe public areas or affordable facilities. In such circumstances, advice alone is unlikely to solve the problem. Institutional decisions can therefore affect entire communities, including people with limited resources.

In my view, the two forms of responsibility are complementary, but institutional action should lead. Public bodies can establish fair conditions, while individuals decide how to use the opportunities provided. A policy is most effective when it combines accessible services with informed personal participation. This division of responsibility avoids blaming individuals for barriers they cannot remove themselves, while still recognising that public programmes depend on engagement and trust. It is therefore more realistic to ask institutions to create fair opportunities and residents to participate in ways that suit their circumstances.
original_model_responses.annotation: Both views receive development before the writer gives a reasoned judgement.

original_model_responses.title: Model: advantages and disadvantages of digital services
original_model_responses.prompt: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of the growing use of digital public services.
original_model_responses.response:
Digital public services can make everyday administration faster and more convenient, but their expansion also raises questions about access and reliability. On balance, the advantages are considerable, although they depend on whether non-digital alternatives remain available.

One clear benefit is efficiency. People may complete routine tasks without travelling to an office or waiting for an appointment. This can save time for users and allow public employees to focus on cases that require direct attention. Digital systems can also make information easier to update and distribute, reducing the risk that different offices provide inconsistent instructions.

However, online services may exclude people who lack reliable internet access, suitable devices or confidence using digital tools. Technical failures can also interrupt essential services, while poorly protected systems create privacy and security risks. These disadvantages are particularly serious when a digital platform becomes the only route to support.

The benefits therefore outweigh the drawbacks only when services are designed inclusively. In addition, digital systems should be introduced gradually, with clear instructions and accessible support, so that people who are less confident with technology are not left behind during the transition. Clear complaints procedures are also necessary for users who encounter errors. Governments should provide accessible interfaces, protect personal data and retain telephone or face-to-face help for those who need it. Digital delivery should improve access rather than make assistance conditional on technical ability. Regular user testing, clear privacy rules and staff support are therefore as important as the software itself; otherwise, a system designed for efficiency may create new forms of exclusion.
original_model_responses.annotation: The essay compares both sides and makes the judgement conditional, not absolute.

original_model_responses.title: Model: congestion and practical measures
original_model_responses.prompt: Many cities face increasing traffic congestion. What problems does this cause, and what measures could address it?
original_model_responses.response:
Growing traffic congestion creates problems that extend beyond longer journeys. It affects the environment, reduces economic efficiency and can make urban life less predictable. Addressing it requires more than simply building additional roads; cities need reliable alternatives to private car use.

One consequence is the loss of time. When roads are heavily congested, workers and businesses cannot plan journeys accurately, and deliveries become less dependable. Traffic also increases local air pollution and noise, which can reduce residents’ quality of life. These effects are not distributed equally: people living near major roads may experience the greatest exposure, even if they do not own a car.

A practical response is to improve the frequency, coverage and affordability of public transport. If buses and trains provide dependable connections, some commuters may choose them instead of driving. Safe walking and cycling routes can also make short journeys less car-dependent. In the busiest areas, carefully designed parking policies or congestion charges may encourage a shift, although such measures should be accompanied by affordable alternatives so that lower-income residents are not unfairly burdened.

No single measure will remove congestion entirely. A combination of better public transport, safer active travel and fair demand management is more likely to reduce traffic while preserving access to jobs and services. The effectiveness of each measure should be assessed through journey reliability, affordability and local air-quality indicators, rather than road speed alone. Reviews should be published so residents can judge whether the chosen measures improve journey reliability and access, rather than merely shifting traffic from one street to another. This is especially important when new charges affect people who have few alternatives.
original_model_responses.annotation: The response links each proposed solution to a problem and notes an equity risk.

original_model_responses.title: Model: why a trend is growing and what it may mean
original_model_responses.prompt: More people are choosing to study online. Why is this happening, and what effects may it have on education?
original_model_responses.response:
Online study has become more common because digital platforms offer flexibility and can connect learners with courses that may not be available locally. This shift can widen access, but it may also change the way students participate and receive support.

A major reason for the growth of online learning is convenience. Learners can often choose when to study and avoid the cost or time associated with travelling to an educational institution. Online platforms may also provide access to specialist teachers, recorded explanations and materials that can be revisited. For adults who combine education with work or family responsibilities, this flexibility can make further study possible.

The effects are mixed. On the positive side, students can learn at a pace that suits their needs and may benefit from a wider range of resources. However, online education can reduce informal interaction with teachers and classmates. Learners who have limited internet access, unsuitable study conditions or weak self-management skills may find it difficult to remain engaged. The quality of online courses also varies, so access to a platform does not automatically guarantee effective learning.

Overall, online study is likely to remain an important part of education because it offers genuine flexibility. Its value will depend on course design, student support and whether institutions provide alternatives for learners who cannot study effectively online. A blended model may therefore be preferable in subjects that require discussion, practical feedback or supervised work, while fully online provision can remain useful for flexible content-based study. Teachers can review these supports as learners become more confident, gradually reducing guidance while keeping help available when a student encounters a new difficulty.
original_model_responses.annotation: Both parts of the question are answered in separate, developed sections.

stage27.pedagogy: Task-focused Academic Writing practice. Official exam descriptors inform the learning checklist; local checks are heuristic and never claim to assign an IELTS band.
stage27.data_policy: All 84 in-app Task 1 datasets are original fictional practice datasets. Real-world reading and data sources are linked separately for idea-building and evidence literacy; figures are not copied or represented as real statistics.
stage27.rights_policy: No copyrighted publisher tests, paid book scans, protected audio, model scripts or password-protected companion files are bundled. The platform links to official sources and supports the learner’s own licensed study copies.
stage27.language_policy: Uzbek for navigation, explanations and study instructions; English for IELTS prompts, source material, model responses and writing output.
stage27.scoring_policy: Internal criterion review uses four 0–10 practice ratings. Task 2 is weighted twice as much as Task 1 for the combined practice index. This is not an official IELTS band score.
stage27.limitations: Local writing audit is rule-based. It cannot fully evaluate relevance, argument validity, factual accuracy, naturalness or assign an official examiner band.

Official IELTS Academic and British Council practice pages are linked from the corresponding core skill studios.

stage35.name: Academic Content & Assessment Excellence

reading.method: Power Lab challenge submission requires an answer, exact passage quote for normal answers, and reason. NOT GIVEN requires an absence rationale and no external knowledge.

listening.method: Power Lab challenge submission requires the day MP3 to be played and a phrase that matches the scripted source. Audio is synthetic original IELTS Boost practice, not official IELTS audio.

vocabulary.local_curator: Source URL/title, English definition, Uzbek sense, original example, POS, sense note, optional US/UK IPA and separate CEFR source URL; learner-reviewed overrides saved locally with JSON import/export.
vocabulary.cefr_policy: Inherited levels remain estimates; a learner must check and record a sense-level source before assigning a verified CEFR label.

stage35.quality_policy: No automatic IELTS examiner band is generated. Local 0–10 values are practice metrics. Official IELTS descriptors are paraphrased as guidance and linked to rights holders; no protected tests, audio or publisher text were copied.

game_engine.scoring: 0–10 internal formative learning score; never an IELTS band

speaking.live_transcript: Web Speech API where the Android/browser supports it; manual transcript fallback included
speaking.pronunciation: Must be reviewed from audio; not generated from transcript

vocabulary.definitions_and_uzbek_translation: On-demand external lookup with local cache where available; machine translation labelled provisional

pwa.install_ui: beforeinstallprompt where supported; Chrome menu fallback

stage36.storage: Original local storage key retained; Stage36 additions stored under state.stage36 and Speaking reports; export a backup before upgrading.

readingSourcePacks.title: The urban food equation: shorter journeys, larger systems
readingSourcePacks.focus: Separate local benefits from whole-system energy costs.

sources.title: National Geographic · Urban Farming Is Growing a Green Future
The Guardian · Are indoor vertical farms really future-proofing agriculture?
Project Drawdown · Deploy Vertical Farms

readingSourcePacks.passage:
Cities are often described as consumers rather than producers of food. Yet urban agriculture includes more than allotments and rooftop vegetable beds. It ranges from community gardens and greenhouse projects to highly controlled indoor farms in which crops are stacked vertically. These approaches share a location, but they do not share the same technology, costs or environmental consequences.

Growing food close to consumers can shorten some supply chains. It may also create educational opportunities, local employment and green spaces. Vegetation on roofs can provide shade, retain some rainwater and contribute to urban cooling. Such benefits are especially relevant in neighbourhoods where access to green space is limited. However, the distance between a farm and a customer is only one part of a food product’s environmental footprint.

A controlled indoor farm can produce crops throughout the year and use water carefully. It can also protect plants from some pests and weather extremes. The trade-off is that artificial lighting, heating, cooling, pumps and monitoring systems require energy and equipment. If the electricity comes from carbon-intensive sources, a short delivery journey may not compensate for the energy used inside the building. A system can therefore be efficient in land or water terms while remaining energy-intensive.

Outdoor urban plots face a different set of constraints. Land is expensive, and soil near former industrial sites may contain contaminants that must be tested and managed before food is grown. Community gardens can improve neighbourhood life, but rising property values may make an area less affordable for the residents who helped create the space. A project that is environmentally attractive can still have unequal social effects.

The evidence does not support one universal model. A rooftop greenhouse, a neighbourhood garden and a fully enclosed vertical farm should be assessed against different objectives. Decision-makers need to ask what is being produced, how much energy is required, where that energy comes from, who can access the food and what land use is being displaced. Urban farming is best understood as one part of a wider food system, not as a single technology capable of solving food security on its own.

questions.question: Which statement best expresses the passage’s central argument?
options: Urban farming is beneficial only when crops are grown on rooftops.
Different forms of urban farming offer different benefits and costs, so they must be assessed as part of a wider food system.
Indoor farms are always more environmentally friendly than outdoor farms.
Transport distance is the only reliable measure of a food system’s environmental impact.
questions.evidence: The evidence does not support one universal model.
questions.explanation: The conclusion rejects a single universal solution and calls for whole-system assessment.

questions.question: The passage states that every urban farm uses artificial lighting.
questions.evidence: A controlled indoor farm can produce crops throughout the year and use water carefully.
questions.explanation: The passage distinguishes indoor farms from rooftop plots and community gardens; it does not say every type needs artificial lighting.

questions.question: What may soil near former industrial sites contain?
questions.evidence: soil near former industrial sites may contain contaminants that must be tested and managed before food is grown.
questions.explanation: The answer is stated directly in the paragraph about outdoor urban plots.

readingSourcePacks.title: Migration routes: how birds navigate a changing world
readingSourcePacks.focus: Distinguish established routes, navigation cues and research tools.

sources.title: National Geographic · Bird migration is one of nature’s great wonders
National Geographic · Why warblers face an increasingly treacherous spring migration

readingSourcePacks.passage:
Animal migration is not simply movement from one place to another. It is a repeated journey linked to feeding, breeding and seasonal conditions. For many birds, the route is shaped by more than distance: suitable resting places, weather, predators and the timing of food availability all affect the journey.

Many migratory birds travel at night. Darkness can mean smoother air currents, while the stars and other celestial cues provide orientation. Birds also use established flyways: broad routes that connect breeding and wintering areas and offer opportunities to stop and refuel. These routes are not empty corridors. Several species may share them, and the same landscape can become a critical pause in the journey for different populations.

Navigation appears to combine several mechanisms. Experiments and field observations suggest that birds can use the position of the sun, stars and Earth’s magnetic field. Experience may also matter. Young birds sometimes travel with older individuals or learn from social cues, although the relative importance of inherited behaviour and learning remains an active research question. A single explanation is unlikely to account for every species and migration pattern.

Technology has changed what researchers can observe. Small tracking devices can record movement and environmental conditions, while radar can reveal large-scale patterns that would be difficult to document by watching individual birds. These tools do not automatically explain why a bird chose a route, but they allow researchers to compare journeys across seasons and locations.

Climate change adds another layer of uncertainty. If temperature, wind or the timing of insect emergence changes, birds may arrive at a familiar place when the food supply is no longer at its usual peak. A shift in migration dates may therefore be beneficial in one situation and harmful in another. The most useful studies combine tracking with observations of habitat and food. The route itself is only part of the story; survival depends on what birds encounter along the way.

questions.question: Which paragraph describes technology used to observe migration at a large scale?
questions.evidence: Technology has changed what researchers can observe. Small tracking devices can record movement and environmental conditions, while radar can reveal large-scale patterns that would be difficult to document by watching individual birds.
questions.explanation: The technology paragraph is D.

questions.question: Does the writer claim that inherited behaviour alone explains how all birds navigate?
questions.evidence: A single explanation is unlikely to account for every species and migration pattern.
questions.explanation: The writer explicitly rejects one explanation for all species.

questions.evidence: Birds also use established flyways: broad routes that connect breeding and wintering areas and offer opportunities to stop and refuel.
questions.explanation: The missing word is repeated exactly in the passage.

readingSourcePacks.title: Language evolution: evidence, gaps and competing explanations
readingSourcePacks.focus: Separate established observations from hypotheses about human language origins.

sources.title: British Council · How humans evolved language (C1)
The Guardian · Stop making sense: focus on sounds to help learn a language

readingSourcePacks.passage:
Human language is remarkable not because other animals are silent, but because people can combine words and grammatical patterns to communicate about events that are distant, hypothetical or abstract. Researchers can compare the structures of languages and reconstruct parts of their history. Explaining how the human capacity for language emerged is more difficult, because speech itself rarely leaves a fossil.

Archaeological evidence can show that early humans made tools, organised activities and produced symbolic objects. It cannot, by itself, reveal the exact sentences they could speak. Physical remains offer a different kind of clue. The development of the mouth, throat and tongue may indicate when humans became capable of producing a wider range of sounds, but sound production alone does not demonstrate the presence of modern grammar.

The brain is central to the debate. Language depends on several capacities working together: memory, planning, pattern recognition, motor control and the ability to learn shared conventions. A larger brain does not automatically explain how these abilities emerged. Researchers therefore investigate the development of neural systems as well as the social environments in which communication became useful.

Genetics may provide additional evidence, but it is not a simple answer. A genetic change can influence the development of a biological pathway without determining a complex cultural skill on its own. The same caution applies to animal communication. Studies of other species can reveal sophisticated signalling and, in some cases, sensitivity to ordered patterns. That does not make their communication systems identical to human language.

The strongest account is likely to combine biological capacity with social learning. Children acquire language through repeated exposure, interaction and feedback; the same general principle helps explain why adults benefit from hearing unfamiliar sounds in meaningful contexts. Yet researchers must keep distinct questions separate: how humans became capable of speech, how languages diversified, and how individuals learn a new language today. Evidence that answers one question should not be treated as proof of another.

options: Why archaeological remains cannot preserve speech

Why animal signals are identical to human grammar
A complete genetic explanation of language
questions.evidence: Language depends on several capacities working together: memory, planning, pattern recognition, motor control and the ability to learn shared conventions.
questions.explanation: The paragraph focuses on multiple cognitive systems, not a single factor.

questions.evidence: It cannot, by itself, reveal the exact sentences they could speak.
questions.explanation: The passage distinguishes artefacts from direct evidence of speech.

questions.explanation: Any one of the three body parts is accepted.

readingSourcePacks.title: Mohenjo-daro: what urban design can and cannot prove
readingSourcePacks.focus: Evaluate archaeological evidence and distinguish observation from interpretation.

sources.title: National Geographic · Did this ancient society thrive without elites?

readingSourcePacks.passage:
Mohenjo-daro was one of the major urban centres of the Indus Valley, or Harappan, civilisation. Its remains reveal a planned settlement with organised streets, drainage systems and buildings made from standardised bricks. Some houses had access to wells and drainage, suggesting that water management was built into everyday urban life rather than added as an afterthought.

Such features invite questions about how the city was governed. Standardised construction may indicate shared rules, specialised production or coordination across neighbourhoods. It does not, on its own, identify who made the decisions. Archaeologists have long debated whether the Indus cities were governed by powerful elites, councils, administrators or a different arrangement that is difficult to recognise through material remains.

One reason the debate continues is the absence of certain kinds of evidence. Excavators have not found obvious palaces, royal tombs or monumental statues comparable to those associated with rulers in some other ancient societies. However, the absence of a familiar symbol of authority does not prove that authority did not exist. Political power can be expressed through control of trade, ritual, access to water or the organisation of labour, all of which may leave less immediately recognisable traces.

The Indus script remains undeciphered, which limits what researchers can learn from written records. Objects and buildings therefore carry much of the burden of interpretation. Their distribution, dimensions and patterns can support hypotheses, but several explanations may fit the same evidence. A regular street plan might reflect central planning; it might also result from shared building conventions adopted by many communities.

The responsible conclusion is cautious. Archaeology can identify patterns and rule out some explanations, but it rarely provides a complete picture of social life. New excavations and better comparisons may change the debate. The most useful question is not simply whether Mohenjo-daro was equal or unequal, but what kinds of evidence would allow researchers to test competing accounts of how decisions were made.

questions.question: The passage states that Mohenjo-daro had an undeciphered writing system.
questions.evidence: The Indus script remains undeciphered, which limits what researchers can learn from written records.
questions.explanation: The statement agrees with the text.

questions.evidence: Excavators have not found obvious palaces, royal tombs or monumental statues comparable to those associated with rulers in some other ancient societies.
questions.explanation: The discussion of missing elite symbols appears in Paragraph C.

questions.evidence: The Indus script remains undeciphered
questions.explanation: The noun is stated directly.

readingSourcePacks.title: Nature’s calendar: when biological clocks fall out of step
readingSourcePacks.focus: Understand cause, timing, exceptions and uncertainty in climate impacts.

sources.title: National Geographic · Nature is out of sync—and that’s reshaping everything

readingSourcePacks.passage:
Phenology is the study of seasonal events in nature: flowering, leaf emergence, insect activity, breeding and migration. These events are connected. A plant may flower when temperatures reach a particular range; an insect may emerge when its host plant is available; a bird may time its arrival to coincide with an abundance of insects. The calendar is biological as well as human.

Long-term observations can reveal changes that a single season would hide. Researchers who return to the same field site year after year can compare flowering dates, animal behaviour and local weather. Such records are valuable because they show patterns across time. They are not perfect, however. A change in one species does not necessarily mean that an entire ecosystem has shifted in the same way.

Warming can move seasonal events earlier, but the consequences vary. An animal that becomes active earlier may gain extra feeding opportunities if food is available. Another species may be disadvantaged if its food source or breeding habitat does not respond at the same rate. This mismatch is one reason scientists study relationships between species rather than measuring temperature alone.

The phrase “nature is out of sync” describes a possible pattern, not a universal outcome. Some populations may benefit in the short term; others may lose access to food or face new competition. Local altitude, rainfall, snow cover and habitat can alter the result. Even within one species, individuals in different locations may respond differently.

Phenological research therefore depends on repeated measurements and careful interpretation. Scientists need to distinguish a trend from an unusual year, and correlation from causation. The aim is not to produce a single date for “the season”, but to understand how connected biological events respond when environmental conditions change. Long datasets can guide conservation decisions, although uncertainty remains about how several interacting changes will combine in the future.

questions.question: Which term describes the study of seasonal events in nature?
questions.evidence: Phenology is the study of seasonal events in nature: flowering, leaf emergence, insect activity, breeding and migration.
questions.explanation: The definition appears in the opening sentence.

questions.question: Does the writer suggest that every species benefits when seasonal events occur earlier?
questions.evidence: Some populations may benefit in the short term; others may lose access to food or face new competition.
questions.explanation: The writer explicitly says effects differ.

questions.question: A mismatch can occur when a species’ food source does not respond at the same ______.
questions.evidence: Another species may be disadvantaged if its food source or breeding habitat does not respond at the same rate.
questions.explanation: The missing word is “rate”.

readingSourcePacks.title: Feedback that changes performance
readingSourcePacks.focus: Identify actionable feedback and the difference between praise and evidence.

sources.title: British Council · C1 reading resources
British Council · Giving and receiving positive feedback

readingSourcePacks.passage:
Feedback is often treated as a comment delivered after a task. In effective learning, it is better understood as information that helps a learner decide what to do next. A general statement such as “good work” may encourage someone, but it does not explain which part of the work was successful or how the learner can repeat that success.

Useful feedback is specific, connected to a clear goal and delivered while the work can still be improved. In a reading task, for example, a learner may choose the correct answer but rely on a guess. A stronger review asks the learner to locate the sentence that supports the answer, identify the paraphrase in the question and explain why the competing option is wrong. The focus moves from the final mark to the reasoning that produced it.

Feedback also needs to distinguish different problems. A learner may misunderstand a word, overlook a contrast marker, confuse the writer’s view with a reported opinion or fail to follow a reference across sentences. These errors require different repairs. Repeating the same question may strengthen memory for the answer, but it may not repair the underlying skill. A better retest changes the example while keeping the target skill constant.

The person receiving feedback has a role as well. Learners need to compare a comment with their own work, decide whether it is justified and record a next step. This makes feedback a dialogue rather than a judgement. Teachers, peers and automated tools can all contribute, but each source has limits: a tool may identify a pattern without understanding the full argument, while a human reviewer may have limited time or inconsistent standards.

The most productive cycle is therefore short and evidence-based: attempt, inspect, explain, repair and transfer. Progress is demonstrated not by the number of comments received, but by the learner’s ability to avoid the same type of mistake in a new context.

options: To reward a learner after every task
To provide information that guides the learner’s next action
To ensure that every error receives the same correction

questions.explanation: The passage defines feedback by its forward-looking function.

it may not repair the underlying skill.
it removes the need for evidence.

questions.explanation: The correct ending preserves the contrast in the text.

questions.explanation: The answer is the evidence-bearing sentence.

readingSourcePacks.title: Work and wellbeing: why a single productivity measure is not enough
readingSourcePacks.focus: Compare measures and recognise trade-offs in social research.

sources.title: British Council · B2 reading resources (Work–life balance)
IELTS Academic Reading format

readingSourcePacks.passage:
Work is often measured through hours, output or income. These indicators are useful, but none captures the whole experience of working life. Two people may work the same number of hours and produce similar results while experiencing very different levels of control, security, fatigue or satisfaction.

A single measure can therefore create a misleading comparison. Long hours may indicate a demanding job, but they may also reflect flexible scheduling or a temporary period of intense activity. High output may suggest efficiency, yet it can conceal unpaid work, poor conditions or costs transferred to families and communities. Researchers need to define what they mean by productivity before comparing groups.

Work-life balance is also not a fixed ratio between time at work and time outside it. A person’s responsibilities, commute, health, income and access to support shape what balance means in practice. Policies that offer flexibility may help some employees but create uncertainty for others if working hours become unpredictable. The same policy can therefore have different effects depending on the context.

Good research makes these differences visible. It can combine quantitative indicators, such as hours and wages, with interviews or diaries that show how people experience work. Qualitative evidence does not replace measurement; it explains what a number may leave out. Researchers should also identify whose experiences are missing from a sample. A survey of full-time office workers, for example, may not represent carers, informal workers or people with multiple jobs.

The practical lesson is to avoid treating one indicator as a complete description of wellbeing. Decisions about work should use several measures, state the limits of each and consider how benefits and costs are distributed. A useful policy is not simply one that increases output; it is one whose effects can be examined across different groups and over time.

questions.evidence: Two people may work the same number of hours and produce similar results while experiencing very different levels of control, security, fatigue or satisfaction.
questions.explanation: The passage directly contradicts “necessarily the same”.

The case for removing all measurement

questions.explanation: The paragraph advocates mixed evidence.

questions.evidence: Researchers should also identify whose experiences are missing from a sample.
questions.explanation: The answer appears in the paragraph on research design.

readingSourcePacks.title: Asteroids: from distant objects to manageable risks
readingSourcePacks.focus: Distinguish hazard, probability, observation and risk response.

sources.title: British Council · B2 reading resources (Asteroids)
NASA · Near-Earth Object Observations

readingSourcePacks.passage:
Asteroids are rocky bodies left over from the formation of the Solar System. Most orbit the Sun in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, but some travel on paths that bring them relatively close to Earth. Their existence does not mean that an impact is imminent. Risk depends on several factors, including an object’s size, orbit, composition and the probability that its path will intersect Earth.

Astronomers search for near-Earth objects by observing the sky repeatedly. A single observation can reveal a moving point of light, but it is not enough to determine a precise orbit. Additional measurements taken over time help researchers calculate where an object is likely to travel. As the observational record improves, the uncertainty in the predicted path can shrink. In some cases, a preliminary estimate that appears concerning becomes less so after more data are collected.

This process illustrates the difference between a hazard and a risk estimate. An object may be physically capable of causing damage, yet the probability of an impact during a particular period may be extremely low. Scientists must communicate both the potential consequence and the level of uncertainty. Presenting only the worst possible outcome can create unnecessary alarm; presenting only a low probability can hide why continued observation matters.

Planetary defence includes more than finding objects. Researchers also study how an asteroid might respond to a change in motion. A small alteration made sufficiently early could, in principle, shift the location where an object would otherwise arrive. Timing is essential: a modest intervention years in advance may be more useful than a much stronger attempt made too late. Any proposed response would require reliable tracking and careful international coordination.

The wider lesson is that scientific preparedness is built from repeated observation, transparent uncertainty and plans that can be reviewed as evidence changes. The aim is not to predict every event with certainty, but to reduce the chance that an avoidable surprise becomes a disaster.

questions.question: Why is one observation insufficient to calculate an asteroid’s precise orbit?
options: Researchers need additional measurements over time.
Asteroids cannot be detected with telescopes.
The asteroid belt is too close to Earth.

questions.explanation: Repeated observations improve the orbital estimate.

questions.explanation: The writer cautions against worst-case-only communication.

questions.evidence: A small alteration made sufficiently early could, in principle, shift the location where an object would otherwise arrive.
questions.explanation: The intervention changes the object’s motion.

readingSourcePacks.title: Eridu and the problem of reconstructing ancient cities
readingSourcePacks.focus: Trace how physical remains support historical reconstruction.

sources.title: National Geographic · How archaeologists found one of the oldest cities on earth

readingSourcePacks.passage:
An ancient city is rarely discovered as a complete picture waiting to be read. Archaeologists usually encounter layers: traces of buildings, discarded objects, repairs, empty spaces and later construction. Each layer records a different moment, and the challenge is to work out how those moments relate to one another.

Eridu, in southern Mesopotamia, illustrates the difficulty. A mound can contain debris left by repeated occupation, but the visible shape of the mound does not reveal the full plan of the settlement. Excavation, mapping and the study of pottery or building materials help researchers identify phases of activity. The evidence may suggest that a place was used for a long time, even when the exact purpose of every structure remains uncertain.

The condition of a site also shapes the record. Later buildings may cover earlier ones; water, wind and human activity can move or destroy material. A lack of an object is not always proof that it was never present. It may have been removed, reused or simply not found in the area that has been excavated. Archaeologists therefore distinguish between what the evidence shows and what remains unknown.

Historical interpretation becomes stronger when different kinds of evidence agree. A building’s location may suggest a relationship with a water source; its materials may point to trade or local production; written records, where available, may add names or administrative details. Yet written sources also have perspectives and omissions. They may describe the priorities of rulers rather than the lives of ordinary residents.

The most reliable reconstruction is therefore provisional. New evidence can change the interpretation of a site, and competing explanations should be tested against the same material. Archaeology does not simply recover the past; it builds and revises explanations about it. Recognising uncertainty is not a weakness of the discipline but a condition of responsible historical reasoning.

questions.question: Which paragraph explains how later activity can alter the archaeological record?
questions.evidence: Later buildings may cover earlier ones; water, wind and human activity can move or destroy material.
questions.explanation: This evidence is in Paragraph C.

questions.question: The passage states that every structure at Eridu has a known purpose.
questions.evidence: The evidence may suggest that a place was used for a long time, even when the exact purpose of every structure remains uncertain.
questions.explanation: The passage says some purposes remain uncertain.

questions.question: Archaeologists distinguish between what evidence shows and what remains ______.
questions.evidence: Archaeologists therefore distinguish between what the evidence shows and what remains unknown.
questions.explanation: The exact word is “unknown”.

readingSourcePacks.title: Listening to sounds: a neglected dimension of language learning
readingSourcePacks.focus: Understand research claims, sample limits and practical implications.

sources.title: The Guardian · Stop making sense: focus on sounds to help learn a language

readingSourcePacks.passage:
Language lessons often place visible words at the centre of study. Learners memorise vocabulary, review grammar and practise writing sentences. These activities are important, but the sound system of a language can receive less deliberate attention. The ability to distinguish unfamiliar sounds may influence how easily a learner recognises and produces words.

A study discussed by The Guardian in October 2026 examined auditory precision among Japanese learners of English. The report describes 67 learners and tasks involving differences in pitch, duration and tone, including vowel contrasts that do not occur in the same way in Japanese. Brain imaging was used alongside behavioural tasks to examine how participants processed unfamiliar sounds. The findings suggested that learners who were more accurate at hearing subtle differences tended to acquire unfamiliar pronunciation more successfully.

The result should not be interpreted as evidence that some nationalities are naturally poor at learning languages. A small study can reveal a relationship worth investigating, but it cannot explain every learner’s progress or separate all influences. Exposure, teaching methods, motivation, age, practice opportunities and individual experience may all matter. The reported findings are therefore a reason to pay attention to sound perception, not a basis for ranking groups of learners.

For teaching, the practical implication is straightforward. Learners can compare minimal pairs, notice where a sound changes meaning, listen for duration and stress, and repeat short phrases after checking what they actually heard. The aim is not to imitate an accent perfectly. It is to improve the ability to hear distinctions that carry meaning and to make speech more intelligible.

A balanced programme combines listening discrimination with vocabulary, grammar, reading and interaction. Sound awareness is neither a substitute for language knowledge nor a minor extra. It is one component of a system, and it deserves explicit practice when learners struggle to distinguish or produce unfamiliar contrasts.

readingSourcePacks.title: Coral reefs: restoration is more than planting fragments
readingSourcePacks.focus: Separate restoration techniques from ecosystem-wide recovery.

sources.title: The Guardian · Coral reporting and restoration coverage
National Geographic · Science and nature features

readingSourcePacks.passage:
Coral reefs are built by small animals whose calcium-carbonate structures create complex habitats. These habitats support many forms of marine life and can protect coastlines by reducing wave energy. Their condition depends on several interacting factors, including water temperature, water quality, light, disease and the availability of suitable surfaces for young corals to settle.

Restoration projects often begin with a visible intervention: growing coral fragments in nurseries and attaching them to damaged reef areas. Such work can help replace lost structures and test methods for increasing survival. Yet planting fragments is not the same as restoring an ecosystem. A reef also depends on fish, algae, microbes, water movement and the surrounding habitat. If the pressures that damaged the reef continue, newly planted corals may struggle to survive.

Some projects experiment with less familiar methods. Researchers and conservation groups may use sound, artificial structures or carefully selected coral strains to influence settlement and survival. These techniques can be promising, but results from a small site should not be treated as proof that the method will work everywhere. Local conditions and species composition matter.

Effective restoration therefore starts with diagnosis. Is the main pressure heat stress, pollution, destructive fishing, sediment or a combination? The answer affects what intervention is appropriate. In some places, protecting remaining healthy reef may produce greater benefits than attempting large-scale replanting. In others, restoration may be useful when combined with reduced local pressures and long-term monitoring.

Success should be measured beyond the number of fragments installed. Researchers can examine survival, growth, biodiversity and the return of ecological functions over time. This broader approach makes restoration less dramatic but more informative. It recognises that a reef is a living system, not simply a surface that can be repaired by replacing missing pieces.

readingSourcePacks.title: Food waste: the hidden emissions in what is never eaten
readingSourcePacks.focus: Trace indirect impacts along a supply chain and evaluate policy responses.

sources.title: Project Drawdown · Reduce Food Loss & Waste
British Council · Sustainable supermarkets (C1)

readingSourcePacks.passage:
Food waste is not only a question of discarded meals. When food is lost before it is eaten, the resources used to grow, process, package, transport and store it are wasted as well. The climate impact can therefore begin long before a product reaches a household bin.

Loss occurs at several stages. Crops may be damaged or rejected during harvesting and storage. Food can be spoiled while being transported or processed. Retailers may remove products that no longer meet appearance standards, while households may buy more than they can use. These causes are not identical, so a single policy is unlikely to solve them all.

The distinction between food loss and food waste can help identify where action is needed. Loss is often associated with production, handling and distribution; waste is frequently used for food discarded by retailers, food services or consumers. The boundary between the terms varies across studies, so reports should define their categories before comparing estimates.

Possible responses include better storage, clearer date labels, improved forecasting, redistribution of safe surplus food and changes in purchasing habits. Each measure has conditions. Redistribution requires safe handling and a recipient network; improved packaging may reduce spoilage but create additional material use; discounts may help products sell but do not necessarily address the reasons consumers over-purchase.

A systems approach asks where the greatest avoidable losses occur and which intervention changes the underlying process. It also avoids treating all discarded food as equally preventable. Some waste is difficult to eliminate, but much can be reduced through coordination between growers, retailers, charities and households. Progress should be measured with transparent definitions and data across the supply chain, not only by counting what appears in a supermarket’s waste bin.

options: Because only household bins produce emissions.
Because the resources and emissions used earlier in production and distribution are also wasted.
Because discarded food is always transported internationally.
Because packaging is the only source of emissions.

assessment.weight: Four IELTS speaking criteria are equally weighted in official assessment.
assessment.local_scale: 0–10 self-review sliders are internal practice ratings only; never convert them to an official IELTS band.
assessment.pronunciation_rule: Only review pronunciation after listening to actual audio. Accent imitation is not a goal; intelligibility and use of phonological features matter.
assessment.transcript_rule: Transcript checks are text-only heuristics; they cannot reliably measure fluency, intelligibility, stress, intonation or pronunciation.

recording.method: Browser MediaRecorder + IndexedDB when the browser grants microphone permission and the page is served in a secure context (HTTPS or localhost).
recording.fallback: Manual transcript and self-review; do not report an audio recording as saved unless IndexedDB confirms the write.
recording.asr: Optional browser SpeechRecognition where supported; transcript is a draft and recognition accuracy is not a pronunciation score.

speakingExpert.copyright_policy: Only original practice prompts are embedded. Official descriptors and external samples are linked rather than copied as full protected materials.

policy.cefr: All legacy B2/C1 labels are estimates, not official CEFR certification; validate word senses in Cambridge English Vocabulary Profile / Oxford Learner word lists.
policy.ipa: Legacy IPA may include eSpeak machine-generated fields. Treat IPA as a guide, verify the exact sense and pronunciation using learner dictionaries and audio.
policy.translation: Only bundled, contextualised English definitions, Uzbek glosses, examples and parts of speech are used in the 84-day core set. Online machine translations are provisional until checked by the learner.
policy.copyright: Use external dictionaries and official word lists through their own websites. Do not copy full dictionary entries or protected wordlists into the platform.

index_expansion.coverage: Pronunciation-only index. American pronunciation converted from CMU ARPABET to broad IPA; British IPA, definition, Uzbek translation, example, POS and CEFR are not supplied for these added items.
index_expansion.license_note: CMUdict repository license and attribution are included in the resource map. This is a pronunciation index, not an IELTS or CEFR vocabulary syllabus.
